title: Western Air Express 7
summary: A Boeing 247D on approach to Burbank crashed on 12 January 1937 after encountering severely reduced visibility from heavy rain and fog. The aircraft descended below safe altitude and struck a mountain ridge, impacting with the left wing tip first and skidding approximately 125 feet before coming to rest. One passenger died immediately and three others died within a week.

factors.evidence: severely lowered visibility due to heavy rain and fog
aircraft off-course, on approach in severely lowered visibility, and suddenly spotting a ridge looming directly ahead
off-course Boeing 247D, en route from Salt Lake City, was on approach
aircraft struck the ground with the left wing tip, skidded along the mountainside for approximately 125 feet

events.text: Boeing 247D NC13315 approaching Burbank in severely reduced visibility from heavy rain and fog
Pilot William L. Lewis suddenly spots ridge looming directly ahead and cuts power to engines to pancake onto hillside
Aircraft strikes left wing tip and skids along mountainside for 125 feet at elevation 3550 feet near summit of Los Pinetos, coming to rest headed opposite direction from impact

title: Hindenburg disaster
summary: The Hindenburg, a hydrogen-filled rigid airship, arrived at Lakehurst on 6 May 1937 after crossing the Atlantic from Frankfurt. During the docking procedure with the mooring mast, the airship caught fire and burned rapidly, destroying the structure. Thirty-five passengers and crew plus one person on the ground were killed. The disaster shattered public confidence in giant rigid airships.
probable_cause: Hydrogen fuel ignited during mooring attempt at Lakehurst. Exact cause of ignition remains disputed.

factors.evidence: Hydrogen-filled airship burned rapidly during docking with mooring mast
The hydrogen-filled airship caught fire and was destroyed during its attempt to dock
Airship structure destroyed, marking the abrupt end of the airship era

events.text: Hindenburg crossed Atlantic from Frankfurt and passed over Boston on morning of May 6
Airship was hours behind schedule and diverted to wait for afternoon thunderstorms to pass
Directed back to Lakehurst to make landing after being notified storms had passed
The hydrogen-filled airship caught fire and was destroyed during its attempt to dock with its mooring mast at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, causing 35 fatalities among the 97 people on board

notes: Exact cause of ignition remains disputed
Multiple theories proposed for ignition source

title: 1937 Beert KLM Douglas DC-2 crash
summary: A Douglas DC-2 operated by KLM crashed near Beert, Belgium, on 28 July 1937 shortly after departing Brussels on the final leg to Paris. An explosion and fire broke out in the passenger cabin while the aircraft was climbing to 400 meters, likely initiated by an electrical short circuit in combination with highly flammable nitrocellulose-based interior materials and combustible film stock aboard. The aircraft crashed in a potato field near Halle, killing all 15 occupants. Medical examination indicated death resulted from smoke inhalation before impact.
probable_cause: An in-flight fire in the passenger cabin caused by a probable electrical short circuit igniting highly flammable interior materials. The aircraft carried nitrocellulose-based insulation and combustible film stock which rapidly propagated the fire.

factors.evidence: Investigators considered a short circuit in electrical wiring as a probable cause of the fire, particularly in combination with leaking fuel.
The aircraft interior contained nitrocellulose-based materials and highly combustible film stock, allowing rapid fire propagation.
A fire broke out in the passenger cabin during flight at approximately 400 meters altitude, followed by loss of control.
The intense fire caused structural failure and the aircraft crashed into a potato field near the railway station.

events.text: Aircraft departed Schiphol Airport with two passengers aboard, bound for Brussels intermediate stop.
Aircraft departed Brussels with nine additional passengers (total 11) for final leg to Paris in rain showers.
Aircraft reached altitude of approximately 400 meters after takeoff.
Explosion believed to have occurred during flight in the passenger cabin.
Burning aircraft crashed into potato field near railway station near Halle southwest of Brussels.
All 15 occupants killed; victims died from smoke inhalation before aircraft impact.

notes: Exact cause of ignition not definitively established; confidence medium due to multiple possible causes (electrical short, passenger lighter)

title: Sabena OO-AUB Ostend crash
summary: A Junkers Ju 52/3m SABENA flight from Munich to London scheduled to stop at Frankfurt, Brussels and Ostend diverted to Stene Aerodrome near Ostend due to bad weather. At 14:47 local time the aircraft struck the chimney of a brick factory and crashed, bursting into flames, killing all 12 on board. A Belgian official enquiry concluded that a passenger, Grand Duchess Cecilie, gave birth during flight, and the pilot was attempting emergency landing because of this medical emergency.
probable_cause: A Belgian official enquiry concluded the pilot was attempting to land at the aerodrome despite poor weather conditions because one of the passengers, the Hereditary Grand Duchess Cecilie who was 8-months pregnant, gave birth during the flight. The aircraft struck a brick factory chimney at 2:47 p.m., causing the crash.

factors.evidence: bad weather caused the flight to divert to Stene Aerodrome instead of the scheduled stop at Ostend Airport
one passenger, Grand Duchess Cecilie, gave birth during flight which was the reason pilot was attempting to land despite poor weather
Aircraft hit the chimney of a brick factory and crashed at 2:47 p.m. local time
